q: One-rescuer infant CPR. What compression technique does this recap want for the test?

opts.why: New AHA: one-hand heel for one-rescuer infant CPR. Two fingers were not getting depth.
Two-finger is the old method. The update is one-hand heel.
Two-thumb encircling is preferred for two-rescuer infant CPR, not one rescuer.
Adult two-hand is not the infant one-rescuer default here.

q: Two-rescuer infant or child CPR. Preferred compression technique?

opts.why: Two-thumb encircling stays preferred for two-rescuer infant or child CPR.
One-hand heel is the one-rescuer infant update, not the two-rescuer preference.
Two-finger is not the two-rescuer preferred method.
Adult two-hand is not the preferred infant two-rescuer grip.

q: What chest compression fraction does this recap want you to hit?

opts.why: CCF floor is 60%. Target is ≥80%. A 10% rise in CCF is about an 11% rise in survival.
60% is the floor, not the target. Aim for 80% or more.
Those numbers are below the recap’s 60% floor.
80% is the target, not the floor. The floor is 60%.

q: How long may a compression pause last in this recap?

opts.why: Never interrupt compressions for more than 10 seconds if you can help it.
15 seconds is over the 10-second cap.
20 seconds is over the 10-second cap.
30 seconds is over the 10-second cap.

q: Routine mechanical CPR (Lucas) in this recap?

opts.why: AHA does not recommend routine mechanical CPR. Setup pauses interrupt compressions and worsen outcomes.
They don't tire, but routine use is still not recommended. Setup pauses hurt.
Depth and rate stay consistent, but routine use is still not recommended.
Setup is the problem: long pauses. Routine use is not recommended.

q: Which DNR does this recap treat as a reason not to start CPR?

opts.why: A valid original, state-specific DNR that is physically present. A photo is not enough.
A photo does not count here. You need the original in hand.
Rigor is a do-not-start sign, but it is not a DNR. This stem is the DNR rule.
Dependent lividity is a do-not-start sign, but it is not a DNR.

q: STOP mnemonic. What does S stand for here?

opts.why: S is Starts breathing and has a pulse (ROSC). Then you stop compressions.
S needs breathing AND a pulse. Breathing without a pulse is still arrest.
S needs breathing AND a pulse. Pulse without breathing is not the S in STOP.
Transferred is T in STOP, not S.

q: Adult respiratory arrest (pulse present). Breath rate in this recap?

opts.why: Adults: 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 per minute). Child and infant is 1 every 2–3 seconds.
Every 2–3 seconds is the child and infant rate, not adult.
That is too slow. Adult is every 6 seconds.
It is 1 breath every 6 seconds, not 2.

q: They are choking but still coughing and moving air. What do you do?

opts.why: Mild obstruction: hands off. Let them cough. Do not start thrusts yet. Oxygen is fine.
Thrusts are for severe obstruction, not a patient who is still moving air.
Back blows are for severe obstruction. Mild still coughing: hands off.
Chest thrusts are the infant or pregnant/obese severe rule, not mild obstruction.

q: A choking patient goes unresponsive. After 30 compressions you look in the mouth. Blind finger sweep?

opts.why: Pull only what you can easily see and safely grab. No blind finger sweeps. Then 2 breaths.
Do not sweep blindly. Only remove a visible object.
Compress first, then look, then breaths.
You do look after compressions. You just do not sweep blind.

q: Obvious opioid overdose in arrest or respiratory failure. Naloxone vs ABCs?

opts.why: They die of hypoxia. Ventilate or do CPR first. Naloxone is secondary after ABCs.
Do not delay the airway and oxygen for the drug.
If they are pulseless, they still need CPR.
Address ABCs now. Then naloxone per protocol.

q: An advanced airway is in. How do you ventilate during CPR in this recap?

opts.why: Asynchronous CPR: compressions 100–120 with no 30:2 pause. 1 breath every 6 seconds.
Drop 30:2 once the advanced airway is in.
Do not stop compressions for breaths after an advanced airway.
That is the child respiratory-arrest range, not asynchronous adult CPR breaths.
